page.text:
A bare mathematical set is an unstructured collection of points,
possessing neither geometry, hierarchy, nor internal dynamics. To breathe
mathematical life into a set, one must specify how its elements interact.
This is the fundamental role of a *relation*.

Formally, a binary relation on a set $X$ is realized simply as a subset
of the Cartesian product $X \times X$. Yet despite this austere
set-theoretic definition, relations embody the primary structural motifs
of all modern mathematics:
- *Equivalence relations* model symmetry, grouping elements into clusters
  of indistinguishability that collapse to form quotient structures.
- *Order relations* model hierarchy and precedence, organizing elements
  into partially or totally ordered posets and lattices.
- *Functions*—the subject of the following chapter—are single-valued
  relations that govern dynamics and transformations.
